summary: Publishes the information needed to build interoperable applications on the OpenPGP format. It describes the packet formats and methods needed to read, check, generate, and write conforming messages, but does not cover storage or implementation questions. It is a standards-track document, replaced by RFC 9580.

plainLanguage.summary: This is the rulebook for the packages used to lock and sign messages. If every program follows it, they can all open each other's locked messages.

subtitle: The packet formats that let OpenPGP software encrypt, sign and exchange keys and messages in an interoperable way.

tldr.problem: Software that encrypts and signs data needs a precisely defined message and key format, so that different programs can read each other's output.
tldr.mechanism: OpenPGP builds messages and keys from tagged packets. A random session key encrypts the data, public-key encryption protects that session key, signatures are separate packets, and an optional Radix-64 'ASCII armor' makes the binary data safe to paste into text channels.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4880 replaced RFC 2440 and RFC 1991 and was itself later obsoleted by RFC 9580. It was also updated by RFC 5581.

today: RFC 4880 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 9580, which is now the current OpenPGP specification. It was also updated by RFC 5581, and it replaced RFC 1991 and RFC 2440.

sections.title: What OpenPGP Provides
sections.content:
RFC 4880 describes the message-exchange packet formats used by OpenPGP for encryption, decryption, signing and key management. It revises RFC 2440, which itself replaced RFC 1991. OpenPGP is based on PGP 5.x, part of the PGP family of software created by Philip R. Zimmermann.

The core technologies are digital signatures, encryption, compression and Radix-64 conversion. Implementations SHOULD compress a message after signing it and before encrypting it. The RFC covers key management only in part and leaves details such as keyring storage out of scope.

Although the specification requires both encryption and signatures, it accepts that subset implementations may omit encryption and still be useful for signature-only applications.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a rulebook for sending secret and signed messages, so that programs from different makers can understand each other.

sections.title: How Encryption and Signing Work
sections.content:
OpenPGP combines two kinds of encryption. The sender generates a random session key for each message and uses it with a symmetric cipher to encrypt the data. That session key is then encrypted with each recipient's public key, and these encrypted session keys come first in the message. The recipient decrypts the session key with their private key, then decrypts the message. A message can also be keyed from a passphrase.

For a signature, the sender hashes the message, signs the hash with the private key and attaches the result. The receiver hashes the message again and verifies the signature. When both are used, the signature is made first, and then the message with its signature is encrypted.

Passphrases become keys through a string-to-key (S2K) specifier. The three types are simple, salted, and iterated and salted. Implementations SHOULD use salted or iterated-and-salted S2K, because simple S2K is more vulnerable to dictionary attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: You lock the message with a one-time key, then lock that key inside a smaller box that only your friend can open. A signature is like your personal stamp, which anyone can check.

sections.title: Packets and Their Headers
sections.content:
An OpenPGP message, key or certificate is a sequence of packets. Each packet has a header and a body. The first header octet is the Packet Tag, which says what kind of packet follows and how the length is written. Bit 7 is always one, and bit 6 marks the new packet format. The new format is RECOMMENDED unless compatibility with PGP 2.6.x is needed, and tags of 16 or above MUST use it.

New-format lengths use one octet for bodies up to 191 octets, two octets for 192 to 8383, or five octets (the first being 255) for up to 4,294,967,295. Partial Body Lengths let data of unknown size be sent as a stream; the first partial length MUST be at least 512 octets and they are only allowed for literal, compressed and encrypted data packets.

The defined tags include 1 (Public-Key Encrypted Session Key), 2 (Signature), 3 (Symmetric-Key Encrypted Session Key), 4 (One-Pass Signature), 5 to 7 and 14 (secret and public keys and subkeys), 8 (Compressed Data), 9 (Symmetrically Encrypted Data), 11 (Literal Data), 13 (User ID), 18 (Integrity Protected Data) and 19 (Modification Detection Code).
sections.plainLanguage: Every piece of an OpenPGP message is wrapped in a labelled envelope. The label says what is inside and how long it is.

sections.title: Keys, Signatures and Messages
sections.content:
A transferable public key starts with one Public-Key packet, followed by revocation signatures, one or more User ID packets (each followed by certification signatures), optional User Attribute packets and optional subkeys. Each subkey MUST be followed by a binding signature from the top-level key. A signing subkey's binding signature MUST include an embedded signature from the subkey back to the primary key.

Signature packets come in versions 3 and 4. Implementations SHOULD accept V3 and SHOULD generate V4, which carries extensible subpackets. Signature types include signatures over binary and text documents (0x00, 0x01), certifications of a User ID (0x10 to 0x13), subkey binding (0x18), key revocation (0x20) and timestamps (0x40). OpenPGP leaves final judgement of validity to the receiver, so the certification types are deliberately loose.

A V4 fingerprint is the 160-bit SHA-1 hash over the public-key packet, and the eight-octet Key ID is its low-order 64 bits. Key IDs can collide, so implementations SHOULD NOT assume they are unique. V3 keys and MD5 are deprecated.

A message follows a small grammar: an encrypted message, a signed message, a compressed message or a literal message, and decrypting or decompressing must yield a valid OpenPGP message again.
sections.plainLanguage: A key is like an ID card with your name, some stamps from people who vouch for you, and spare keys for different jobs. Each spare key is tied back to the main one.

sections.title: ASCII Armor and Cleartext Signatures
sections.content:
OpenPGP data is binary, and some channels only carry seven-bit printable text. Radix-64 (ASCII armor) fixes this. It is the MIME base64 encoding plus a 24-bit CRC written as four characters after an equals sign. The armor wraps the data in header and tail lines such as BEGIN PGP MESSAGE, BEGIN PGP PUBLIC KEY BLOCK and BEGIN PGP SIGNATURE, with five dashes on each side. Radix-64 data lines are limited to 76 characters. Armor headers such as Version and Comment are not protected by any signature.

The cleartext signature framework signs text while leaving it readable. The text sits between a BEGIN PGP SIGNED MESSAGE line and an armored signature. Lines that begin with a dash MUST be dash-escaped by prefixing them with a dash and a space, and trailing spaces and tabs are removed before signing.
sections.plainLanguage: Binary data is like a picture that some mail slots cannot take. Armor turns it into plain letters, like a code written out in words, so it fits through any slot.

sections.title: Integrity Protection and Security Notes
sections.content:
Plain CFB encryption cannot reliably detect tampering. OpenPGP therefore defines the Modification Detection Code (MDC). In a Symmetrically Encrypted Integrity Protected Data packet (tag 18), a 20-octet SHA-1 hash of the plaintext is appended in an MDC packet (tag 19) and encrypted with it. Implementations MUST support decrypting these packets and SHOULD prefer generating them. Any MDC failure MUST be treated as a security problem, not merely a data problem.

The RFC explains that this was designed as a lighter integrity check than a signature, one that keeps deniability. The motivating threat is an attack published in 2002 by Jallad, Katz and Schneier, in which a modified message is sent to a user whose returned decryption acts as an oracle for the attacker.

Other notes: MD5 is deprecated and implementations MUST NOT generate new MD5 signatures; implementations MUST implement SHA-1, TripleDES, DSA for signatures, Elgamal for encryption and uncompressed data. PKCS#1 padding errors should not be reported differently from decryption errors, and the weakest algorithm in a message should still be strong enough for the purpose.
sections.plainLanguage: A tamper seal on a jar tells you if someone opened it. The MDC is that seal for an encrypted message, and a broken seal must be taken seriously.

items.label: Public-Key Encrypted Session Key
items.desc: Holds the session key encrypted to a recipient's public key.

items.label: Signature
items.desc: Binds a public key to some data.

items.label: Symmetric-Key Encrypted Session Key
items.desc: Session key protected by a passphrase-derived key.

items.label: Integrity Protected Data
items.desc: Encrypted data protected by an MDC.

items.label: Modification Detection Code
items.desc: SHA-1 hash used to detect modification.

items.label: Salted S2K
items.desc: Adds an 8-octet salt to the hash input.

items.label: Iterated and Salted S2K
items.desc: Salt plus passphrase hashed repeatedly up to an octet count.

items.label: Private/Experimental
items.desc: Reserved for private or experimental use.
